text: July 6th, 1960. A 79 year old man dies in Geneva. He leaves behind the most famous watch brand on Earth, and he leaves it to nobody. He started out as an orphan from a small town in Bavaria. He ended up building the watch that movie stars, deep sea explorers, and half of all rap lyrics are obsessed with. Today, analysts estimate Rolex sells about 10 billion Swiss francs of watches a year, around 1.2 million watches. That's one new Rolex, roughly every 27 seconds. And yet nobody owns Rolex. No shareholders, no stock price, no billionaire air with a yacht named after a watch. So where does all that money go? The answer starts with a grieving widower and ends with a charity that hands out hundreds of millions a year without making a sound. Khrumbach Bavaria, 1881. Hans Wyrstowff is born into a family of hardware merchants. At 12, he loses his mother. A few months later, his father. His uncles sell the family business and lock the money away until the kids grow up. Not exactly a Disney intro. Although to be fair, Disney intros are mostly orphans. He moves to London and in 1905, at 24, he starts a watch company with his brother-in-law, Alfred Davis, Vistoff and Davis. Catchy. We'll fix that later. His big bet? The wristwatch. Here's the thing. Back then real men carried pocket watches. wristwatches were small, inaccurate and seen as jewelry for women. A watch on your wrist? Yes. Like a bracelet? Like the future. Sir, I would sooner wear a skirt. This stuff doesn't care. He's convinced the wristwatch will take over. He just needs two things. A name and proof. The name first. He says he combined letters every possible way, got about 100 names and none of them worked. Then one morning riding on the top deck of a horse drawn bus through the city of London in his own words, a genie whispered in his ear. Rolex. Short. Easy to say in any language. Looks good on a dial. In 1908 the name is registered. Branding department, one guy, one bus, one genie. Now the proof. In 1910 a Rolex becomes the first wristwatch in the world to earn the Swiss certificate of chronometric precision. Translation, an official accuracy test, like a driving exam but for watches. Then in 1914 the Q Observatory in England gives a tiny Rolex a Class A certificate. That's a test usually reserved for big marine chronometers on ships, 45 days, 5 positions, 3 temperatures, and the little wristwatch passes. The bracelet just beat the boat clocks. But then comes World War I. Britain slaps heavy taxes on luxury imports and duties on the gold and silver used for watch cases. So, in 1919, WillStorff packs up and moves the company to Geneva. Tax planning, 1919 style. And this is where it gets interesting. Watches back then had a weakness. Water and dust got inside and killed them. In 1926 Rolex patents a case with a screwed down bezel, back, and crown. The little knob you wind it with. Sealed shut, like an oyster. So he calls it the oyster. Naming is clearly his superpower now. But how do you prove a watch's waterproof in 1927? You find someone crazy enough to to swim the English Channel. Enter Mercedes Glitz, a typist from London. On October 7th, 1927, she swims the Channel. But then, another woman claims a faster swim and doubts spread. So two weeks later, Glitz gets back in the water to prove herself. This time, a gold Rolex oyster hangs on a ribbon around her neck, more than 10 hours in cold water. And the watch still ticking, totally dry inside. Willstorff doesn't waste it. On November 24th, 1927, Rolex buys the front page of the daily mail, the wonder watch that defies the elements. Influencer marketing almost a century before Instagram. In 1931, the perpetual rotor. Trans, the watch winds itself every time your wrist moves. In 1945, the date just, with the date that changes on its own. But then came the darkest chapter. World War II. British officers captured by Germany have their watches taken away. So Willstorff makes them an offer. Right to Rolex through the Red Cross, order a watch, and pay after the war. He reportedly told them, you must not even think of settlement during the war. Officers in the camps ordered as many as 3,000 watches. One oyster please, I'll pay you after the war. Of course sir, and if we lose the war, then sir, the invoice will be the least of our problems. Generous, patriotic, and honestly, the greatest customer loyalty program ever invented. Then in 1944, his wife Florence dies. They have no children, no errors. So Willstorff does something almost no founder does. He creates a foundation, the Hans-Wilstoff foundation. Translation, a kind of charity that can own things but has no owners itself. And he arranges for it to own Rolex when he dies, his entire stake goes to it. Fast forward to January 23, 1960, the deep sea submersible Trieste dies to the bottom of the Marianaiana trench, 10,916 meters, the deepest point on the planet. Strap to the outside, a Rolex. When it comes back up, the watch works perfectly. The explorer Jacques Picard sends a telegram to Geneva. Your watch works as well at 11,000 meters as it does on the surface. Less than six months later, on July 6th, 1960, Hans Vistoff dies. The orphan from Bavaria leaves his empire to a foundation and Rolex officially belongs to nobody. So what happens to a company with no owner? It gets bigger, much bigger. October 26th, 2017, New York. Paul Newman's own Rolex Daytona, a gift from his wife, goes up for auction. It sells for $17.8 million. At the time, the most expensive wristwatch ever sold at auction. For a watch that tells you the time, just like your phone. In 2023, Rolex buys Bûchava, a famous watch retailer it had worked with since 1924. And according to estimates from Morgan Stanley and Luxe Consult, in 2024, Rolex sold about 10.5 billion Swiss francs of watches, roughly a third of the entire Swiss watch market. Rolex itself publishes no accounts. Peak mystery. How much for Rolex? It's not for sale. Everything is for sale. Not this. Nobody owns it. Then who do I talk to? Nobody. Here's the trick. No shareholders means nobody calling every three months asking for more growth. Translation? Rolex can think in decades, not quarters. It can make fewer watches than people want. And waiting lists are the best advertising money can't buy. And the foundation? According to its own figures, it pays about 75 million francs in taxes a year, and in one recent year it gave out more than 500 million francs in aid, housing, education, social causes, mostly in Geneva. Its motto, translated from French, good does not make noise and noise does no good. Very Swiss. So what's the lesson? Sometimes the most powerful thing a founder can do is make sure nobody can ever cash out. An orphan who had no errors built a company that can never be inherited, never be sold, and never stops ticking. If you enjoyed this, subscribe.
